notes: Ruling slot 22 holds the United Thai People's Party, the governing party Thanom chairs. Slot 13 (template partner) holds the civil-bureaucratic establishment of the cabinet technocrats, using MD's Amart sprite. Army hardliners around Praphas and Narong are the catchy Khana Patiwat in 7. CIA-built Border Patrol Police in 0. Patani: BRN 11 (MD), BNPP 12.

0.name: Tamruat Trawen Chaidaen
0.text:
The Border Patrol Police were created in the early 1950s with American advisers and CIA funding to guard Thailand's frontiers. Their elite Police Aerial Reinforcement Unit has trained Hmong irregulars in Laos, and the force now leads counter-insurgency in the hill country of the north and northeast.

It is the most American-shaped arm of the Thai state, bound to Washington through training, aircraft and money, and to the palace through royal patronage of its village schools. Its leverage lies in its remote outposts, intelligence networks and its role at the heart of the secret war next door.

1.name: Phak Prachathipat
1.text:
The Democrat Party, founded in 1946, is Thailand's oldest party and the main parliamentary opposition. Revived under the 1968 constitution and led by former Prime Minister Seni Pramoj, it swept Bangkok in the February 1969 election and holds the second largest bloc in the House.

It stands for parliamentary government, civil liberties, the monarchy and a market economy, and is firmly anti-communist and pro-American. Its base is the Bangkok middle class, civil servants and southern provinces, and its leverage lies in the press and in the capital's demand for an end to military tutelage.

2.name: Sangkhomsat Parithat
2.text:
Social Science Review is the liberal journal founded in 1963 by the writer Sulak Sivaraksa, which has become the main forum for critical thought permitted under military rule. Academics, writers and young graduates from Thammasat and Chulalongkorn use its pages to debate development, corruption and the American presence.

It calls for constitutional government, a free press, honest administration and a Thai path that does not simply follow American advice. Its readers are the educated young, and its leverage lies in shaping the ideas of a generation now entering the universities and civil service.

3.name: Luk Sit Pridi
3.text:
Luk Sit Pridi are the veterans of the 1932 revolution, the wartime Free Thai movement and Thammasat University who remain loyal to Pridi Banomyong. The former regent and prime minister has lived in exile in China since 1949, and his followers at home keep a low profile under military rule.

They uphold Pridi's 1933 economic plan, cooperative agriculture, a democratic constitution and a neutral foreign policy, and resent the American alliance. Their influence rests on old networks in the bureaucracy and Thammasat, and on Pridi's standing as the father of Thai democracy.

4.name: Phak Khommiwnit haeng Prathet Thai
4.text:
The Communist Party of Thailand, founded in 1942, launched its armed struggle in August 1965 and on 1 January 1969 organised its guerrillas as the Thai People's Liberation Armed Forces. Directed by a secretive central committee, it operates in the northeast, the northern hills among the Hmong, and the south.

It seeks a people's war to overthrow the military regime and expel American bases, following the line of the Chinese party. Radio Voice of the People of Thailand broadcasts from China, and its strength lies in neglected villages, Hmong grievances and sanctuary across the Lao border.

5.name: Sapha Na Do
5.text:
Sapha Na Do is one of the student discussion groups that have sprung up at Thammasat University, meeting in front of the famous dome to read banned texts. The writings of Jit Phumisak, killed by the authorities in 1966, circulate in mimeographed copies among its members.

Its students attack the military government, the American bases and the feudal legacy of Thai society, and are drawn to Maoist and New Left ideas from abroad. They have no organisation beyond the campus, but their leverage lies in the growing restlessness of tens of thousands of new university students.

6.name: Sai Phibun
6.text:
Sai Phibun gathers the surviving followers of Field Marshal Plaek Phibunsongkhram, who was toppled by Sarit in 1957 and died in exile in Japan in 1964. Among them is Sang Phathanothai, Phibun's former adviser, who opened secret contacts with Zhou Enlai in the 1950s.

They stand for militant Thai nationalism, a strong state and a foreign policy freed from dependence on Washington, including an understanding with Beijing. They have no party, but their leverage lies in old officers, nationalist intellectuals and the regime's growing interest in hedging its bets with China.

7.name: Khana Patiwat
7.text:
Khana Patiwat recalls the junta with which Sarit seized power in 1958 and gathers the officers who see parliament as a dangerous experiment. Its centre is Field Marshal Praphas Charusathien, army commander and interior minister, and Colonel Narong Kittikachorn, Thanom's son and Praphas's son-in-law.

They regard the 1968 constitution as an obstacle to fighting communism and governing efficiently, resent MPs' budget demands and are ready to dissolve the House by decree. Their leverage is the Bangkok garrison, the Interior Ministry and Praphas's command of the army.

8.name: Kudi Charoen Phat
8.text:
The Kudi Charoen Phat in Thonburi is the centre of Thailand's old Twelver Shia community, the Chao Sen, descended from Persian merchants who came to Ayutthaya and whose leading families served the Siamese crown. Its congregation marks Muharram with processions that are part of Bangkok's religious life.

It is loyal to the throne, keeps out of politics and maintains discreet links with Iran. Its influence is small in numbers, but its families have long been integrated into the Thai elite and enjoy access to the court and the bureaucracy.

9.name: Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat
9.text:
The Dawoodi Bohra community of Bangkok is a close-knit congregation of Gujarati traders gathered around their mosque in the old commercial district. Like all Bohras it owes absolute obedience to the Da'i al-Mutlaq, Syedna Mohammed Burhanuddin, who has led the community from Bombay since 1965.

Clergy appointed by the Da'i regulate its religious, commercial and family life, and it avoids open politics. Its strength lies in discipline, communal finance and trading networks reaching across Asia, which answer to its spiritual head rather than to any government.

10.name: Khana Kammakan Klang Islam haeng Prathet Thai
10.native_full: Khana Kammakan Klang Islam haeng Prathet Thai
10.text:
The Central Islamic Committee of Thailand is the state-recognised body for Thai Muslims, headed by the Chularatchamontri, Tuan Suwannasat, who has held the office since 1947. It oversees provincial Islamic committees, mosque registration and religious education under royal patronage.

It preaches loyalty to the King and the Thai state, cooperation with the government and moderation, and counsels Malay Muslims of the south against separatism. Its influence lies in official recognition and the network of mosques, though many Patani Malays regard it as Bangkok's instrument.

11.name: Barisan Revolusi Nasional
11.text:
The Barisan Revolusi Nasional was founded in 1960 by Ustaz Abdul Karim Hassan, a religious teacher from Narathiwat, to free the Malay Muslims of Patani from Thai rule. It builds its network through the pondok religious schools of the southern provinces.

It combines Malay nationalism with Islamic revolution and seeks an independent Patani state ruled by Islamic principles. Its strength lies in teachers and students of the pondoks, the resentment of assimilation policies and sanctuary across the Malaysian border.

12.name: Barisan Nasional Pembebasan Patani
12.text:
The National Liberation Front of Patani was founded in 1959 by Tengku Abdul Jalal, a member of the old Malay aristocracy of the south. It carries on the cause of Haji Sulong, the religious leader who demanded autonomy for Patani in 1947 and disappeared in police custody in 1954.

It seeks self-rule for the Malay Muslims of the southern provinces under Islamic law and Malay culture, appealing to Malaysia and the Muslim world. Its base lies in traditional religious leaders and aristocratic families, and its armed bands operate in the southern hills.

13.name: Kharatchakan
13.text:
Kharatchakan, the servants of the crown, are the senior civil servants and technocrats who actually run the Thai state alongside the generals. Their foremost figures in Thanom's cabinet are Pote Sarasin, former SEATO secretary-general, and Foreign Minister Thanat Khoman.

They favour stability, planned development through the national economic plans and an orderly bureaucracy, and increasingly cautious diplomacy as American commitment in Indochina wavers. Their leverage lies in the ministries, the provincial administration and the palace's trust in an apolitical, royalist officialdom.

14.name: Soi Ratchakhru
14.text:
Soi Ratchakhru takes its name from the Bangkok lane where Field Marshal Phin Choonhavan's family lives, and is the clan network he built with his son Chatichai Choonhavan and son-in-law Pramarn Adireksarn. Pushed aside by Sarit in 1957, they have rebuilt their fortunes in business and diplomacy.

They stand for royalism, private enterprise and the interests of provincial businessmen and landowners, and wait for a return to party politics. Their leverage lies in money, family ties in the army and a network of provincial patrons ready to be turned into a party.

15.name: Chao Sua
15.text:
Chao Sua is the name Thais give to the great Sino-Thai tycoons who dominate banking, rice exporting and trade. The most powerful is Chin Sophonpanich of Bangkok Bank, who like his peers places generals on his boards in exchange for licences and protection.

They favour stability, American-funded growth and close ties to whoever commands the army, and they fear both communism and any democratic campaign against corruption. Their leverage lies in credit, newspapers and the shared profits that bind the Thanom–Praphas regime to big business.

16.name: Thanakhan haeng Prathet Thai
16.text:
The Bank of Thailand, the central bank founded in 1942, has been governed since 1959 by Puey Ungphakorn, an economist of rare integrity who is also dean of economics at Thammasat. Under him the bank has become a stronghold of competent, honest technocrats.

It stands for monetary stability, open markets, private enterprise and fiscal discipline, and quietly resists the generals' demands for easy money. Its leverage lies in its control of credit and the stable baht, and in Puey's moral authority among students and reform-minded officials.

17.name: Samakhom Anurak Sat Pa
17.english: Association for the Conservation of Wildlife
17.text:
The Association for the Conservation of Wildlife was founded by the physician and naturalist Boonsong Lekagul, Thailand's foremost conservationist. It campaigned for the 1960 wildlife protection law and the creation of Khao Yai, the country's first national park, in 1962.

It calls for national parks, protection of forests and endangered species, and an end to hunting by influential officials. Its members are doctors, scientists and educated Bangkok families, and its leverage lies in royal sympathy for conservation and in public outrage at illegal logging and poaching.

18.name: Phak Naeo Ruam Setthakon
18.text:
The Economist United Front Party was formed by Thep Chotinuchit, the veteran leftist deputy from the northeast who was imprisoned under Sarit. It won four seats in the 1969 election, almost all among the poor rice farmers of Isan.

It calls for land reform, rural development, help for indebted farmers and a neutral foreign policy without American bases. Its base is the impoverished northeast, long neglected by Bangkok, and its leverage lies in speaking for a region where communist guerrillas are also seeking recruits.

19.name: Naeo Ruam Rakchat Thai
19.native_full: Naeo Ruam Rakchat haeng Prathet Thai
19.text:
The Thailand Patriotic Front was proclaimed on 1 January 1965 as the united front of the communist-led revolution, gathering exiled politicians, intellectuals and monks alongside party cadres. It works from bases in Laos and China and speaks through the clandestine radio.

It calls for the expulsion of American forces, the overthrow of the Thanom–Praphas dictatorship, a democratic coalition government and neutrality. It follows the Maoist line of protracted people's war, and its leverage lies in appealing to patriots who would never join the Communist Party itself.

20.name: Sayam Rat
20.text:
Siam Rath is the Bangkok daily founded in 1950 by Kukrit Pramoj, the aristocrat, novelist and columnist who is the most popular political voice outside parliament. Through his daily column he shapes opinion among readers far beyond the elite.

It champions the monarchy, Buddhism and Thai national identity, mocks the generals' corruption and warns against both communism and blind dependence on the Americans. Its leverage lies in Kukrit's wit and celebrity, which could turn a newspaper readership into a mass following overnight.

21.name: Kong Asa Raksa Dindaen
21.text:
The Volunteer Defense Corps is the armed village militia founded in 1954 under the Interior Ministry, now commanded through Praphas's ministry. Its volunteers guard villages, district offices and roads in the insurgent provinces of the northeast, north and south.

It indoctrinates rural youth in loyalty to nation, religion and king and treats leftists, separatists and suspected communists as enemies to be destroyed. Its leverage lies in thousands of armed men under direct government control in the countryside, beyond the reach of courts or parliament.

22.name: Phak Saha Pracha Thai
22.text:
The United Thai People's Party was founded in 1968 by the military government to contest the elections of the new constitution. Led by Field Marshal Thanom Kittikachorn, prime minister and supreme commander, with Praphas Charusathien as his deputy, it won the most seats in February 1969 and governs with independents and an appointed Senate.

It stands for the regime of Sarit's heirs: anti-communism, the American alliance and the Vietnam War, development through foreign aid and investment, and firm military control. Its power lies in the armed forces, the bureaucracy and the money of its business allies.

23.name: Ratchawong Chakri
23.text:
The Chakri dynasty has reigned since 1782, and King Bhumibol Adulyadej, on the throne since 1946, has regained much of the prestige lost after 1932 with the encouragement of Sarit. With Queen Sirikit he tours the provinces, sponsors rural development projects and presides over every state ceremony.

The crown stands for national unity, Buddhism and anti-communism, and lends legitimacy to the military governments. Its leverage lies in deep popular reverence, royal patronage of the army and police, and the moral authority to arbitrate when the elite divides.
